claim: Wolbachia are the most widespread bacterial endosymbionts in animals.
source: Wolbachia are the most widespread bacterial endosymbionts in animals.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the scientific literature, supported by the citation context of the manuscript.

claim: Within arthropods, maternally transmitted Wolbachia can selfishly hijack host reproductive processes to increase the relative fitness of their transmitting females.
source: Within arthropods, these maternally transmitted bacteria can selfishly hijack host reproductive processes to increase the relative fitness of their transmitting females.
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific knowledge about Wolbachia reproductive parasitism.

claim: Male killing is one form of reproductive parasitism where infected males are selectively killed.
source: One such form of reproductive parasitism called male killing, or the selective killing of infected males, is recapitulated to degrees by transgenic expression of the prophage WO-mediated killing (wmk) gene.
evidence: This is a definition supported by the literature and the experimental work described in the manuscript.

claim: Transgenic expression of the prophage WO-mediated killing (wmk) gene recapitulates male killing to varying degrees.
source: One such form of reproductive parasitism called male killing, or the selective killing of infected males, is recapitulated to degrees by transgenic expression of the prophage WO-mediated killing (wmk) gene.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from previous work and the current study.

claim: Phylogenetically distant wmk homologs induce no sex-ratio bias in D. melanogaster.
source: While phylogenetically distant wmk homologs induce no sex-ratio bias, closely-related homologs exhibit complex phenotypes spanning no death, male death, or death of all hosts.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3 showing no sex ratio bias for distant homologs.

claim: Closely-related wmk homologs exhibit complex phenotypes spanning no death, male death, or death of all hosts.
source: While phylogenetically distant wmk homologs induce no sex-ratio bias, closely-related homologs exhibit complex phenotypes spanning no death, male death, or death of all hosts.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 2 and 4 showing varying phenotypes.

claim: Alternative start codons in wmk can ablate the killing phenotype.
source: We demonstrate that alternative start codons, synonymous codons, and notably a single synonymous nucleotide in wmk can ablate killing.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Synonymous codons in wmk can ablate the killing phenotype.
source: We demonstrate that alternative start codons, synonymous codons, and notably a single synonymous nucleotide in wmk can ablate killing.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: A single synonymous nucleotide change in wmk can ablate the killing phenotype.
source: We demonstrate that alternative start codons, synonymous codons, and notably a single synonymous nucleotide in wmk can ablate killing.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4 showing that the wSuzi codon variant (one nucleotide change) ablates killing.

claim: Synonymous sequence changes are not necessarily silent in nested endosymbiotic interactions with life-or-death consequences.
source: We conclude that synonymous sequence changes are not necessarily silent in nested endosymbiotic interactions with life-or-death consequences.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data showing phenotypic changes from synonymous mutations.

claim: Male killing selfishly drives the spread of Wolbachia when brothers and sisters compete for limited resources.
source: Male killing selfishly drives the spread of the bacteria when, for instance, brothers and sisters compete for limited resources, and male lethality yields females (the transmitters) a relative fitness benefit due to reduced competition with fewer siblings (Jaenike et al., 2003; Unckless and Jaenike, 2012; Skinner, 1985; Hurst, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous theoretical and empirical work.

claim: Male lethality yields female Wolbachia transmitters a relative fitness benefit due to reduced competition with fewer siblings.
source: Male killing selfishly drives the spread of the bacteria when, for instance, brothers and sisters compete for limited resources, and male lethality yields females (the transmitters) a relative fitness benefit due to reduced competition with fewer siblings (Jaenike et al., 2003; Unckless and Jaenike, 2012; Skinner, 1985; Hurst, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous theoretical and empirical work.

claim: Male killing can cause sex role reversal in hosts.
source: This form of reproductive parasitism can have profound impacts on host behavior and evolution, including a sex role reversal (Jiggins et al., 2000), host nuclear genome changes to resist the phenotype (Majerus and Majerus, 2010; Hornett et al., 2006), and potentially host population extinction (Groenenboom and Hogeweg, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jiggins et al., 2000.

claim: Male killing can cause host nuclear genome changes to resist the phenotype.
source: This form of reproductive parasitism can have profound impacts on host behavior and evolution, including a sex role reversal (Jiggins et al., 2000), host nuclear genome changes to resist the phenotype (Majerus and Majerus, 2010; Hornett et al., 2006), and potentially host population extinction (Groenenboom and Hogeweg, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Majerus and Majerus, 2010 and Hornett et al., 2006.

claim: Male killing can potentially cause host population extinction.
source: This form of reproductive parasitism can have profound impacts on host behavior and evolution, including a sex role reversal (Jiggins et al., 2000), host nuclear genome changes to resist the phenotype (Majerus and Majerus, 2010; Hornett et al., 2006), and potentially host population extinction (Groenenboom and Hogeweg, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Groenenboom and Hogeweg, 2002, and is presented as a potential outcome.

claim: Male killing may be deployed as a control method to crash the population size of arthropod pests and disease vectors.
source: Population modelling also suggests male killing may be deployed as a control method to crash the population size of arthropod pests and disease vectors (Berec et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to population modeling work by Berec et al., 2016.

claim: Male killing can be suppressed by host background.
source: For example, male killing can be suppressed by host background (Majerus and Majerus, 2010; Hornett et al., 2006; Jaenike, 2007; Mitsuhashi et al., 2011), where male hosts exhibit resistance to the phenotype even in the presence of Wolbachia.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations showing host resistance.

claim: Male hosts can exhibit resistance to male killing even in the presence of Wolbachia.
source: For example, male killing can be suppressed by host background (Majerus and Majerus, 2010; Hornett et al., 2006; Jaenike, 2007; Mitsuhashi et al., 2011), where male hosts exhibit resistance to the phenotype even in the presence of Wolbachia.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations showing host resistance mechanisms.

claim: Wolbachia that do not cause male killing in one host species can cause male killing in a second host species upon introgression or transfer to a naïve host.
source: In addition, Wolbachia that do not cause male killing in one host species can cause male killing in a second host species upon introgression or transfer to a naïve host (Jaenike, 2007; Fujii et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jaenike, 2007 and Fujii et al., 2001.

claim: Some Wolbachia strains induce death at different host developmental stages (embryo vs. larvae).
source: Furthermore, some strains induce death at different host developmental stages (embryo vs. larvae) or across different sex determination systems (ZW lepidopterans, XY dipterans, XO arachnids), and the number of surviving males may vary widely (Riparbelli et al., 2012; Sasaki et al., 2002; Zeh et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing variation in timing and extent of male killing.

claim: Some Wolbachia strains induce male killing across different sex determination systems (ZW lepidopterans, XY dipterans, XO arachnids).
source: Furthermore, some strains induce death at different host developmental stages (embryo vs. larvae) or across different sex determination systems (ZW lepidopterans, XY dipterans, XO arachnids), and the number of surviving males may vary widely (Riparbelli et al., 2012; Sasaki et al., 2002; Zeh et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies across different host taxa.

claim: The number of surviving males in male-killing infections may vary widely.
source: Furthermore, some strains induce death at different host developmental stages (embryo vs. larvae) or across different sex determination systems (ZW lepidopterans, XY dipterans, XO arachnids), and the number of surviving males may vary widely (Riparbelli et al., 2012; Sasaki et al., 2002; Zeh et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: wmk (WO-mediated killing) was identified as a male-killing candidate gene from prophage WO in the wMel Wolbachia strain of Drosophila melanogaster.
source: We recently identified a male-killing candidate gene, wmk (WO-mediated killing), from prophage WO in the wMel Wolbachia strain of Drosophila melanogaster based on comparative genomic, transgenic, and cytological approaches (Bordenstein and Bordenstein, 2016; Perlmutter et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: Wmk is a putative transcription factor with two predicted helix-turn-helix (HTH) DNA-binding domains.
source: It is a putative transcription factor with two predicted helix-turn-helix (HTH) DNA-binding domains, and transgenic expression in D. melanogaster embryos recapitulates many cytological and molecular aspects of male killing including accumulation of DNA damage in male embryos that overlaps with sites of dosage compensation activity (Riparbelli et al., 2012; Perlmutter et al., 2019; Harumoto et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic prediction and supported by citations.

claim: Transgenic expression of wmk in D. melanogaster embryos recapitulates many cytological and molecular aspects of male killing.
source: It is a putative transcription factor with two predicted helix-turn-helix (HTH) DNA-binding domains, and transgenic expression in D. melanogaster embryos recapitulates many cytological and molecular aspects of male killing including accumulation of DNA damage in male embryos that overlaps with sites of dosage compensation activity (Riparbelli et al., 2012; Perlmutter et al., 2019; Harumoto et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental work.

claim: Transgenic wmk expression causes accumulation of DNA damage in male embryos that overlaps with sites of dosage compensation activity.
source: It is a putative transcription factor with two predicted helix-turn-helix (HTH) DNA-binding domains, and transgenic expression in D. melanogaster embryos recapitulates many cytological and molecular aspects of male killing including accumulation of DNA damage in male embryos that overlaps with sites of dosage compensation activity (Riparbelli et al., 2012; Perlmutter et al., 2019; Harumoto et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to cytological studies.

claim: The wmk gene and two cytoplasmic incompatibility factor (cif) genes occur nearby specifically in the eukaryotic association module (EAM) of prophage WO.
source: The wmk gene and two cytoplasmic incompatibility factor (cif) genes that underlie cytoplasmic incompatibility (a parasitism phenotype whereby offspring die in crosses between infected males and uninfected females) occur nearby specifically in the eukaryotic association module (EAM) of prophage WO (Bordenstein and Bordenstein, 2016; Perlmutter et al., 2019; LePage et al., 2017), which refers to the phage genome that is inserted into the bacterial chromosome.
evidence: This is supported by citations to genomic analyses.

claim: The EAM is common in WO phages across several Wolbachia strains.
source: The EAM is common in WO phages across several Wolbachia strains (Masui et al., 2001; Wu et al., 2004) and is rich in genes that are homologous to eukaryotic genes or annotated with eukaryotic functions (Bordenstein and Bordenstein, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to comparative genomic studies.

claim: The EAM is rich in genes that are homologous to eukaryotic genes or annotated with eukaryotic functions.
source: The EAM is common in WO phages across several Wolbachia strains (Masui et al., 2001; Wu et al., 2004) and is rich in genes that are homologous to eukaryotic genes or annotated with eukaryotic functions (Bordenstein and Bordenstein, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to genomic annotation work.

claim: The native Wolbachia wmk homologs in wMel, wRec, and wSuzi have nearly identical nucleotide sequences that vary by one to three SNPs.
source: For example, the native Wolbachia wmk homologs in three closely-related strains (wMel of D. melanogaster, wRec of D. recens, and wSuzi of D. suzukii) have nearly identical nucleotide sequences that vary by one to three SNPs (Perlmutter et al., 2019), and yet these strains induce different forms of reproductive parasitism.
evidence: This is supported by citation to sequence analysis.

claim: wMel and wRec induce cytoplasmic incompatibility.
source: wMel and wRec induce cytoplasmic incompatibility, wRec also causes male killing in some strains of a sister species, and wSuzi is not known to induce any reproductive phenotype (Jaenike, 2007; Hamm et al., 2014; Hoffmann, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: wRec causes male killing in some strains of a sister species.
source: wMel and wRec induce cytoplasmic incompatibility, wRec also causes male killing in some strains of a sister species, and wSuzi is not known to induce any reproductive phenotype (Jaenike, 2007; Hamm et al., 2014; Hoffmann, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jaenike, 2007.

claim: wSuzi is not known to induce any reproductive phenotype.
source: wMel and wRec induce cytoplasmic incompatibility, wRec also causes male killing in some strains of a sister species, and wSuzi is not known to induce any reproductive phenotype (Jaenike, 2007; Hamm et al., 2014; Hoffmann, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on wSuzi.

claim: Addition of nine additional amino acids to the N-terminal region of the Wmk protein at the site of a putative alternative start codon ablates the male-killing phenotype.
source: Previous transgenic testing also demonstrated that addition of nine additional amino acids to the N-terminal region of the Wmk protein at the site of a putative alternative start codon ablates the phenotype (Perlmutter et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous experimental work.

claim: The Wmk N-terminus is particularly sensitive to genetic alterations.
source: Therefore, the Wmk N-terminus is particularly sensitive to genetic alterations, which is notable since small modifications such as protein tags in this location are often common additions to proteins that do not typically interfere with function.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that N-terminal additions ablate function.

claim: D. melanogaster does not harbor Wolbachia known to cause male killing.
source: Furthermore, D. melanogaster does not harbor Wolbachia known to cause male killing, although transgenic wmk expression recapitulates the phenotype in this host (Perlmutter et al., 2019), and the wMel strain is most closely-related to the wRec male-killing strain (Metcalf et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about D. melanogaster Wolbachia strains.

claim: Transgenic wmk expression recapitulates male killing in D. melanogaster.
source: Furthermore, D. melanogaster does not harbor Wolbachia known to cause male killing, although transgenic wmk expression recapitulates the phenotype in this host (Perlmutter et al., 2019), and the wMel strain is most closely-related to the wRec male-killing strain (Metcalf et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous experimental work.

claim: The wMel strain is most closely-related to the wRec male-killing strain.
source: Furthermore, D. melanogaster does not harbor Wolbachia known to cause male killing, although transgenic wmk expression recapitulates the phenotype in this host (Perlmutter et al., 2019), and the wMel strain is most closely-related to the wRec male-killing strain (Metcalf et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Some D. melanogaster contain male-killing Spiroplasma symbionts whose plasmid gene Spaid can transgenically recapitulate male killing.
source: In addition, some D. melanogaster contain male-killing Spiroplasma symbionts whose plasmid gene Spaid can also transgenically recapitulate male killing (Harumoto and Lemaitre, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to work on Spiroplasma male killing.

claim: Transgenic expression of wSuzi wmk resulted in death of all expressing flies, both male and female.
source: However, transgenic expression of both homologs unexpectedly resulted in death of all expressing flies, both male and female (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Transgenic expression of wRec wmk resulted in death of all expressing flies, both male and female.
source: However, transgenic expression of both homologs unexpectedly resulted in death of all expressing flies, both male and female (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: HA-wmk transgene exhibited a sex ratio bias comparable to wMel wmk.
source: This transgene, HA-wmk, exhibited a sex ratio bias comparable to wMel wmk, as expected (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Gene expression levels are not significantly different across wSuzi, wMel, wRec, or HA tag wMel wmk transgenes.
source: Gene expression levels are not significantly different across wSuzi, wMel, wRec, or HA tag wMel wmk transgenes, indicating that transcript levels do not account for the phenotypic differences (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Transcript levels do not account for the phenotypic differences between wSuzi, wMel, wRec, and HA-wmk transgenes.
source: Gene expression levels are not significantly different across wSuzi, wMel, wRec, or HA tag wMel wmk transgenes, indicating that transcript levels do not account for the phenotypic differences (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of significant differences in expression despite different phenotypes.

claim: msl-2 transcript levels were comparable across embryos expressing wMel wmk, wSuzi wmk, and wBif wmk.
source: Based on this, we quantified msl-2 transcript levels in embryos expressing wMel wmk (sex ratio bias), wSuzi wmk (all expressing hosts die), and wBif wmk (no killing or sex ratio bias) and found that msl-2 levels were comparable across all genotypes and phenotypes (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: None of the distantly-related wBol1b, wBif, wCaub, or wInn/wBor wmk homologs yield a biased sex ratio when transgenically expressed in D. melanogaster.
source: While transgene expression of wMel wmk induces a biased sex ratio (~one third of expressing males die), none of the more distantlyrelated wBol1b, wBif, wCaub, or wInn/wBor wmk homologs yield a biased sex ratio, demonstrating that they do not recapitulate male killing when transgenically expressed in D. melanogaster under the conditions tested (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Transgene expression of wMel wmk induces a biased sex ratio with approximately one third of expressing males dying.
source: While transgene expression of wMel wmk induces a biased sex ratio (~one third of expressing males die), none of the more distantlyrelated wBol1b, wBif, wCaub, or wInn/wBor wmk homologs yield a biased sex ratio, demonstrating that they do not recapitulate male killing when transgenically expressed in D. melanogaster under the conditions tested (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: wRec and wSuzi wmk transgenes with upstream start codons lost their killing phenotype with no sex ratio bias.
source: As previously observed with other homologs, they lost their killing phenotype with only nine amino acids added to the 5' end of the gene, despite being smaller than many commonly used protein tags (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: All expressing flies survived with no sex ratio bias when wRec and wSuzi wmk were expressed with upstream codons.
source: All expressing flies survived with no sex ratio bias.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Adding the corresponding nucleotides at the 5' end of wRec and wSuzi wmk homologs resulted in predicted differences in RNA secondary structure.
source: Returning to the RNA structure models, we find that simply adding the corresponding nucleotides at the 5' end of each homolog resulted in several predicted differences in RNA secondary structure for each transgene compared to the structures without the additional 5' nucleotides (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on computational RNA structure prediction shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The 16th codon position in wmk segregates among sequences by phenotype.
source: This codon, which codes for Serine in all homologs, segregates among sequences by phenotype.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The HA-wmk and wMel wmk transgenes have a TCG codon at position 16.
source: The HA-wmk and wMel wmk transgenes, which recapitulate male killing, have a TCG codon, while the all-killing transgenes wSuzi and wRec wmk have TCC and AGC, respectively (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in the sequence alignment in Figure 4A.

claim: The wSuzi wmk transgene has a TCC codon at position 16.
source: The HA-wmk and wMel wmk transgenes, which recapitulate male killing, have a TCG codon, while the all-killing transgenes wSuzi and wRec wmk have TCC and AGC, respectively (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in the sequence alignment in Figure 4A.

claim: The wRec wmk transgene has an AGC codon at position 16.
source: The HA-wmk and wMel wmk transgenes, which recapitulate male killing, have a TCG codon, while the all-killing transgenes wSuzi and wRec wmk have TCC and AGC, respectively (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in the sequence alignment in Figure 4A.

claim: The wMel wmk (new) transgene with no changes caused a biased sex ratio.
source: When these three otherwise identical genes were transgenically expressed, the wMel wmk (new) transgene with no changes caused a biased sex ratio as expected; however, and remarkably, expression of transgenes with two different Serine codons ablated the phenotype and resulted in a non-biased sex ratio with normal numbers of expressing flies (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Expression of transgenes with two different Serine codons (wRec codon and wSuzi codon) ablated the male-killing phenotype and resulted in a non-biased sex ratio with normal numbers of expressing flies.
source: When these three otherwise identical genes were transgenically expressed, the wMel wmk (new) transgene with no changes caused a biased sex ratio as expected; however, and remarkably, expression of transgenes with two different Serine codons ablated the phenotype and resulted in a non-biased sex ratio with normal numbers of expressing flies (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: A minimum of one single synonymous site change in the 5' region was sufficient to alter the sex ratio phenotype.
source: Thus, a minimum of one single synonymous site change in the 5' region was sufficient to alter the sex ratio phenotype.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental data showing that the wSuzi codon variant (one nucleotide change) ablates the phenotype.

claim: The nucleotide changes in the codon did not recapitulate the all-killing phenotypes of their corresponding homologs.
source: However, while the nucleotide changes in the codon changed the phenotype, they did not recapitulate the all-killing phenotypes of their corresponding homologs.
evidence: This is based on the observation that the codon swap variants showed no killing rather than all killing.

claim: Mutations even at the synonymous codon and single nucleotide levels can alter the male-killing phenotype.
source: Using a variety of sequences, we report three key results: (i) mutations even at the synonymous codon and single nucleotide levels can alter the male-killing phenotype, (ii) phenotype, genotype, and RNA structural variation exhibit some correlation with each other, and (iii) distantly-related homologs do not induce a male-killing phenotype in transgenic D. melanogaster, while some closely-related homologs from Drosophila species/populations with female-biased sex ratios induce all-killing phenotypes.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Phenotype, genotype, and RNA structural variation exhibit some correlation with each other.
source: Using a variety of sequences, we report three key results: (i) mutations even at the synonymous codon and single nucleotide levels can alter the male-killing phenotype, (ii) phenotype, genotype, and RNA structural variation exhibit some correlation with each other, and (iii) distantly-related homologs do not induce a male-killing phenotype in transgenic D. melanogaster, while some closely-related homologs from Drosophila species/populations with female-biased sex ratios induce all-killing phenotypes.
evidence: This is based on the RNA structure predictions and their correlation with phenotypes.

claim: Distantly-related wmk homologs do not induce a male-killing phenotype in transgenic D. melanogaster.
source: Using a variety of sequences, we report three key results: (i) mutations even at the synonymous codon and single nucleotide levels can alter the male-killing phenotype, (ii) phenotype, genotype, and RNA structural variation exhibit some correlation with each other, and (iii) distantly-related homologs do not induce a male-killing phenotype in transgenic D. melanogaster, while some closely-related homologs from Drosophila species/populations with female-biased sex ratios induce all-killing phenotypes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: Some closely-related wmk homologs from Drosophila species/populations with female-biased sex ratios induce all-killing phenotypes.
source: Using a variety of sequences, we report three key results: (i) mutations even at the synonymous codon and single nucleotide levels can alter the male-killing phenotype, (ii) phenotype, genotype, and RNA structural variation exhibit some correlation with each other, and (iii) distantly-related homologs do not induce a male-killing phenotype in transgenic D. melanogaster, while some closely-related homologs from Drosophila species/populations with female-biased sex ratios induce all-killing phenotypes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2 showing wRec and wSuzi wmk cause all-killing.

claim: Endosymbiont phenotypes of reproductive parasites may not simply be governed by DNA sequence alone.
source: Importantly, this key result implies at the molecular level that endosymbiont phenotypes of reproductive parasites may not simply be governed by DNA sequence alone.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that synonymous changes affect phenotype.

claim: Codon bias varies across species.
source: Indeed, codon bias varies across species (hence the need for codon optimization) (Sharp et al., 1997; Andersson and Kurland, 1990), and there are several mechanisms through which single or few codons can influence transcription or translation.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: When there is a rare codon, there are fewer tRNAs available, and the translation rate may be correspondingly lowered.
source: When there is a rare codon, there are fewer tRNAs available, and the translation rate may be correspondingly lowered (Li et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2012.

claim: There is a bias for rare codons in N-terminal regions of bacterial genes, likely due to their influence on mRNA structure.
source: Notably, there is a bias for rare codons in N-terminal regions of bacterial genes, which is likely due to their influence on mRNA structure (Goodman et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Goodman et al., 2013.

claim: Lower 5' RNA stability or weaker structure can be correlated with ease of initiation and faster translation.
source: Lower 5' RNA stability or weaker structure can also be correlated with ease of initiation and faster translation (Gu et al., 2010), and stem loop structures may affect translation rate in varying ways.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gu et al., 2010.

claim: Strong 5' RNA secondary structure may inhibit ribosomal initiation or translational efficiency.
source: Indeed, strong 5' RNA secondary structure may inhibit ribosomal initiation or translational efficiency (de Smit and van Duin, 1990; Bettany et al., 1989), and there can be selection against SNPs that alter RNA secondary structure (Salari et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to de Smit and van Duin, 1990 and Bettany et al., 1989.

claim: There can be selection against SNPs that alter RNA secondary structure.
source: Indeed, strong 5' RNA secondary structure may inhibit ribosomal initiation or translational efficiency (de Smit and van Duin, 1990; Bettany et al., 1989), and there can be selection against SNPs that alter RNA secondary structure (Salari et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Salari et al., 2013.

claim: There is evidence for selection across the domains of life on codon usage in the first 30–60 nucleotides of a gene, likely due to their impact on mRNA structure near the site of initiation.
source: There is also evidence for selection across the domains of life on codon usage in the first 30–60 nucleotides of a gene, likely due to their impact on mRNA structure near the site of initiation (Gu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gu et al., 2010.

claim: Early codons with low frequencies can be beneficial by slowing elongation, thus preventing ribosome collisions.
source: Additionally, early codons with low frequencies can be beneficial by slowing elongation, thus preventing ribosome collisions, or potentially helping to recruit chaperones to the emerging peptide for proper folding (Tuller et al., 2010; Fredrick and Ibba, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tuller et al., 2010 and Fredrick and Ibba, 2010.

claim: Early codons with low frequencies can potentially help recruit chaperones to the emerging peptide for proper folding.
source: Additionally, early codons with low frequencies can be beneficial by slowing elongation, thus preventing ribosome collisions, or potentially helping to recruit chaperones to the emerging peptide for proper folding (Tuller et al., 2010; Fredrick and Ibba, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations and presented as a potential mechanism.

claim: Some specific codons across the sequence are favored for their lower likelihood of mistranslation.
source: In addition, some specific codons across the sequence are favored for their lower likelihood of mistranslation (Qin et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Qin et al., 2004.

claim: Synonymous codon differences in genes can result in altered gene expression.
source: Indeed, synonymous codon differences in genes can result, for instance, in altered gene expression (Kudla et al., 2009), lower organism fitness (Agashe et al., 2013), or disease (Sauna and Kimchi-Sarfaty, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kudla et al., 2009.

claim: Synonymous codon differences in genes can result in lower organism fitness.
source: Indeed, synonymous codon differences in genes can result, for instance, in altered gene expression (Kudla et al., 2009), lower organism fitness (Agashe et al., 2013), or disease (Sauna and Kimchi-Sarfaty, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Agashe et al., 2013.

claim: Synonymous codon differences in genes can result in disease.
source: Indeed, synonymous codon differences in genes can result, for instance, in altered gene expression (Kudla et al., 2009), lower organism fitness (Agashe et al., 2013), or disease (Sauna and Kimchi-Sarfaty, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sauna and Kimchi-Sarfaty, 2011.

claim: Gene expression levels across representatives of all phenotypes are similar.
source: Beyond codon sequence, gene expression levels across representatives of all phenotypes are similar (Figure 2), supporting post-transcriptional differences as the source of functional variation and refuting the functional redundancy hypothesis in this context.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data in Figure 2.

claim: Post-transcriptional differences are the source of functional variation in wmk phenotypes.
source: Beyond codon sequence, gene expression levels across representatives of all phenotypes are similar (Figure 2), supporting post-transcriptional differences as the source of functional variation and refuting the functional redundancy hypothesis in this context.
evidence: This is inferred from similar expression levels despite different phenotypes.

claim: The functional redundancy hypothesis is refuted in the context of wmk synonymous changes.
source: Beyond codon sequence, gene expression levels across representatives of all phenotypes are similar (Figure 2), supporting post-transcriptional differences as the source of functional variation and refuting the functional redundancy hypothesis in this context.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that synonymous changes affect phenotype despite similar expression.

claim: Codon usage correlates with phenotype in wmk transgenes.
source: Examining the three synonymous transgenes more closely, we find that codon usage indeed correlates with phenotype.
evidence: This is based on analysis of codon frequencies and their correlation with phenotypes.

claim: The original wMel wmk codon at position 16 (TCG) has a frequency of 16.7 per 1000 codons in D. melanogaster.
